evals.prompt: I'm operations director at Second Chapter Thrift, a 501(c)(3) in Spokane, WA whose store funds our adult literacy program (about $1.2M in store revenue). Our donation door is chaos: volunteers accept everything, we're throwing roughly 40% of what comes in into the dumpster, and our hauling bill hit $3,100 last month. Our only guidance online says 'bring your gently used items.' Can you design an intake process for us from the drop-off door through sorting, including what we should be measuring every month?
evals.expected_output: An intake funnel (acceptance, sort, grade, triage into four lanes, receipt) with a published accepted/not-accepted list, sort-station and grading-rubric design, and a monthly dashboard tracking discard and diversion rates plus hauling cost. It should diagnose the high discard rate as mainly an acceptance-policy and donor-communication problem.
assertions: Lays out staged intake decisions covering acceptance, sorting, grading, triage and the donor receipt rather than one undifferentiated donations pile
Routes graded items to distinct lanes including sell-floor, sell-online, salvage/recycle and discard, with discard treated as the last resort
Identifies the vague 'gently used' guidance and the lack of a written accepted/not-accepted items list as the main driver of the 40% discard rate, rather than blaming the graders
Recommends tracking discard rate and diversion rate monthly, measured on the same basis (weight or unit) each month
Recommends adding hauling/tip/recycler fees into the true cost of donation processing
Recommends a sort station physically separate from the sales floor and/or testing electrical items before they reach the floor

evals.prompt: quick one - our volunteers at the Hope Closet resale shop keep arguing about whether a shirt is 'good enough' to put out. two locations, ~60 volunteers. can you just give me a grading system for clothing we can laminate and stick at the sort table?
evals.expected_output: A concise clothing grading rubric with defined tiers (Premium/Boutique, Standard, Value/As-Is, Reject), clear criteria per tier, and the lane each tier routes to, formatted as a one-page station card with a note to add example photos.
assertions: Provides a clothing rubric with distinct named tiers, including a top boutique/premium tier, a standard tier, a value/as-is tier and a reject tier
Gives observable criteria for each tier (e.g., stains, tears, odors, working zippers/buttons, wear level)
Assigns each tier a destination lane, with rejects routed to a textile recycler/salvage rather than straight to the trash except for wet or contaminated items
Recommends adding example photos for each tier on the laminated card to reduce disagreements between volunteers
Suggests routing like-new or designer pieces to a designated reviewer or online review instead of the general rack

evals.prompt: A regular donor dropped off six bags of clothes and a box of kitchen stuff at our Habitat-style resale store in Ohio and asked our volunteer to write '$650' on the receipt so she can deduct it. The volunteer did it. Also our current receipt is just a blank slip with a date. What should our at-donation receipt say, and what do we do about this one?
evals.expected_output: A compliant at-donation receipt template (org name, EIN, date, category description, no value, no-goods-or-services statement) plus guidance that staff should never write a value; the $650 situation should be handed to the in-kind gift acceptance process because it crosses into donor tax valuation and Form 8283 territory.
assertions: Provides a receipt template including the organization's name, EIN and date received, with items described by general category only
States that the organization should not write a dollar value on the receipt and that the donor is responsible for valuing their own non-cash gift
Includes a statement that no goods or services were provided in exchange for the donation
Explains that writing a value at the donor's request turns her valuation into an apparent organizational appraisal and should be stopped through volunteer training

Refers the $650 claim / Form 8283 question to the in-kind gift acceptance process (or nonprofit-in-kind-gift-acceptance) and tells the user to verify current IRS thresholds in IRS Publications 526 and 561
Recommends that a qualified reviewer or the person responsible for gift acceptance check the receipt wording before it is printed, since it is a tax document for the donor

should_not_trigger.query: A donor gave our thrift store a 2015 Honda Civic and wants a receipt showing what it's worth for her taxes. What do we need to send her?
Our sorted donations are piling up on the racks and nothing is moving. How should we set prices and markdowns for donated clothing?
